name: Milan
features: Works fully offline. No account needed to plan a wedding.
A planning board with a guest list and a headcount for each function.
A budget per function, a card showing who has paid what, and a payment timeline by month.
Optional Google sign-in for cloud backup. Sign in only if you want it, nothing required.
More than one wedding on the same device. Create them, switch between them.
No ads. Everything in the first version is free.
oneLine: Works offline, and handles a wedding that's more than one event.

headline: The second one, in build.
subhead: Milan is a wedding planner that works offline, never sells your data, and handles a wedding with more than one function.

sections.heading: One wedding, several functions, one screen.
sections.body: A wedding isn't one event. It's a Sangeet, a Mehendi, a Haldi and the wedding itself, each with a different guest list and a different headcount, and the numbers don't match. Every competitor's store screenshots show the same three screens: a checklist, a budget, a countdown. None of them show the thing that actually makes the planning hard.
sections.closingLine: The planning board puts every function on one screen, with its own list and its own count.

sections.heading: Why it isn't out yet
sections.body: The features are built and verified on real devices. What's left is the short list you'd expect at this stage: the release signing and the launcher icon aren't done. None of it is the kind of thing you rush, and none of it is a reason to put a date on the page.
sections.closingLine: It goes to the store when a person says it's ready, and not before.

privacyPolicy.headline: Privacy policy
intro: This is the privacy policy for Milan, the wedding planner TheGeekDogs builds for Android and iPhone. It is written against the app as it is built today, not against a version that might exist later.

The app needs no account and no network. Everything you plan is written to a database in the app's own private storage on your phone, and that is the only place the app reads from. Nothing leaves the phone unless you sign in and turn on cloud backup, and even then most of it stays. This page says exactly what does.

sections.heading: What is on your phone
body: Your functions and their dates, your planning boards and the options on them, your guest list and its headcounts, your budget, your bookings and every payment you record are stored in a SQLite database inside the app's private storage. The app reads and writes it with the network off, because there is no second place it reads from.

Photos you attach are saved as files in that same private storage. They are not copied to a shared album, to removable storage or to any server. Photos never go to the cloud, including when cloud backup is on.
Uninstalling the app removes all of it. Android and iOS delete an app's private storage along with the app, and unless you signed in there is no other copy of any of it.

sections.heading: Signing in, which you do not have to do
body: Every feature works signed out. There is no signup screen, no email gate, and no part of the app that asks who you are before it opens.

If you want a backup, Settings offers a Google sign-in. Tapping it hands the sign-in to Google and creates an account for you in Firebase Authentication, which is Google's service and the only account system this app uses. That account record holds the email address, name and profile picture of the Google account you picked, because that is what Google writes into it.

The app reads two things out of that record: a stable account identifier, and which provider you used. Your email address is not stored in the app's own data and nothing in your wedding is keyed to it.

sections.heading: Cloud backup
body: Cloud backup does nothing until you sign in, and it exists for one reason: so the same wedding opens on your next phone.

With it on, a copy of your planning data is written to Cloud Firestore, Google's database, filed under your account identifier. That copy covers your boards and the options on them, your guest list including any address, phone number or email address you typed into a guest yourself, your budget lines, your bookings and your payment records. Photos are not part of it.

The copy is yours and only yours. It is not shown to another person, not pooled with anyone else's wedding, and not sold, rented or handed to a third party. This version of the app has no way to share a wedding with another person, so there is nobody it could be shown to.

sections.heading: Your contacts
body: The guest list has an import that reads your phone's contacts. It is the only thing in the app that asks for that permission, it asks the first time you open that import rather than at launch, and the guest list works without it.

The import reads a contact's name and the identifier your phone files it under. It does not read phone numbers, email addresses or postal addresses out of your contacts, and your contact list is never uploaded anywhere.

What it leaves behind is a guest in your own list. If you later type a number or an address onto that guest and cloud backup is on, that guest travels with the rest of your planning data, exactly as a guest you entered by hand would.

sections.heading: The camera, your photos and your calendar
body: The camera and photo library permissions are there so you can put a picture of a venue or an outfit on the board you are deciding it on. Those files stay in the app's private storage.

The calendar permission is one-way. When you export an event, the app hands it to your phone's own calendar app and stops there. It does not read your calendar, and nothing about your calendar reaches us.

sections.heading: Crash reports
body: When the app crashes, Firebase Crashlytics sends a report so the fault can be found. The report carries the device model, the operating system version, the type of the error and the stack trace showing where it happened.

It deliberately does not carry the error's message. A message can quote whatever the app was handling when it failed, and that could be a guest's name, so the app sends the error's type in place of the error itself. No account identifier and no custom values are attached to a crash report either. Both restrictions are enforced by a check that fails the build rather than by anybody remembering them.
Crash reporting is off in development builds.

sections.heading: What the app measures
body: The app sends one product event, through Firebase Analytics. It is called account_slot_interest and it records that somebody tapped one particular row in Settings. It carries no parameters, no identifier of yours and nothing about your wedding.

That is not a promise about restraint, it is what the code can do. An event is a name from a fixed list and nothing else, the wrapper has no way to attach a value to one, and setting a user identifier or a user property anywhere in the app fails the build.

Firebase Analytics also collects its own standard measurements about app usage, such as the device type and an app instance identifier Google generates. That collection is Google's and is described at policies.google.com/privacy.

sections.heading: What the app does not do
body: No ads, and no advertising library in the build. The dependency list is checked against a blocklist that fails the build if one turns up.

Nothing is sold. Nothing is shared with a third party for marketing, profiling or any purpose of their own. The only outside companies involved are Google's services named on this page: Firebase Authentication, Cloud Firestore, Crashlytics and Analytics, each of them doing the job described here and nothing else.
There is no vendor marketplace and no vendor directory. Vendors are notes you keep for yourself. Nothing you write about one is sent to that vendor or to anyone else.
No money moves through the app. Payments are recorded, never processed, so there is no card number, no bank detail and no payment credential in it at any point.

sections.heading: Deleting your data
body: Local data: uninstall the app. The database and the photos go with it.

Cloud data: ask us. The app has no delete control inside it yet, and rather than describe a button that does not exist, there is a page for this — linked at the foot of this policy and from Milan's own page. It opens an email with the request already written; tell us which Google account you signed in with and the cloud copy of your wedding is removed by hand. Uninstalling does not remove it, because it is not on the phone.

Two people read that inbox. A request is acted on within 30 days and usually within a couple of days, and you get a reply when it is done. When a delete control ships inside the app, this page is rewritten the same day and the date at the top of it moves.

sections.heading: Children
body: The app is not directed at children and collects nothing from one knowingly. It has no age field and no account for a child to create. If you think a child has signed in and left data with us, write to the address below and it is removed.

sections.heading: When this page changes
body: If what the app collects changes, this page is updated before that build reaches a store, and the date at the top moves with it. That date is the only version marker on this page and it is the one to check.

contact.heading: Who to write to
body: TheGeekDogs is a two-person mobile studio in Bengaluru, India, and it is the developer and publisher of this app. Questions about this policy, requests to delete cloud data, and anything else on this page go to one inbox, which both of us read.

accountDeletion.headline: Delete your account and your data
intro: Milan needs no account. If you have never signed in, there is no account to delete and nothing of yours is on any server — everything you planned is in the app's own private storage on your phone, and uninstalling the app takes it with it.

This page is for the other case: you signed in with Google and turned on cloud backup, and you want the account and the copy of your wedding that goes with it removed. There is no delete control inside the app yet. Rather than describe a button that does not exist, this is the route that works today, and it is one email.

sections.heading: What gets deleted
body: The account record itself, held by the sign-in service that created it when you tapped Google sign-in. That record is what Google wrote: the account identifier the app uses, and the email address, name and profile picture Google put on it. All of it goes.

The cloud copy of your planning data, held in the cloud database under that identifier. That covers your boards and the options on them, your guest list including any address, phone number or email address you typed into a guest yourself, your budget lines, your bookings and your payment records.
Nothing is kept back as a backup of our own afterwards, and there is no archived copy to restore from. Deletion is not reversible, so ask when you mean it.

sections.heading: What deletion does not touch
body: Your phone. The app's local database is the only thing it reads from, and deleting the cloud copy does not reach into it — your wedding keeps opening, offline, signed out. To remove the local copy as well, uninstall the app: Android and iOS delete an app's private storage along with the app.

Your photos. They were never uploaded. Photos attached to an option are files in the app's private storage and they are not part of cloud backup at all, so there is nothing of them on our side to delete.
Your contacts. The guest-list import reads a contact's name and the identifier your phone files it under, and it uploads nothing. Guests you kept are your own data and they go with the rest of it.

sections.heading: How long it takes
body: A request is acted on within 30 days of it arriving, and in practice within a couple of days: two people read the inbox and the deletion is done by hand.
You get a reply when it is done. If you asked from a different address than the one you signed in with, the reply goes to the address you wrote from.

sections.heading: Afterwards
body: The app signs you out and keeps working. Every feature works signed out — that is the state Milan is built for — so nothing in your planning stops because the account is gone.
Signing in again later creates a fresh account record, with no connection to the deleted one and none of the old data in it.

request.heading: Ask for deletion
body: The link below opens your own mail app with the message already written. It asks for one thing: the Google address you signed in with, which is what identifies the account. Send it from whichever address you like.

Nothing on this page is sent anywhere by the page. There is no form here and it posts to no server — the message is assembled in your browser and only your mail app ever sees it. If your device has no mail app set up, write to the address below by hand and say the same thing.
request.subject: Delete my Milan account and data
bodyLines: Please delete my Milan account and the cloud copy of my wedding data.
The Google account I signed in with:
I understand this removes the account record and the cloud copy, that it cannot be undone, and that anything still on my phone stays there until I uninstall the app.

meta.title: Delete your Milan account | TheGeekDogs
meta.description: How to have your Milan account and the cloud copy of your wedding data deleted. One email, acted on within 30 days, and the app keeps working signed out.
